Using Resources.intro: Humans use the Earth's resources to make materials and products. Understanding sustainable use of resources is crucial for C10.
Using Resources.mnemonic: "Finite Resources Require Smart Development" — Finite, Renewable, Reduce/Reuse/Recycle, Sustainable Development — the core concepts of C10.

🖼️
Diagram: Using Resources

sections.title: Natural and Synthetic Materials
sections.text: Resources come from the natural world or are manufactured from natural materials, and can be finite or renewable.
points: Natural resources — extracted directly from Earth: metals, wood, cotton, limestone, crude oil
Synthetic materials — made from natural resources through chemical processes: plastics, medicines, alloys, fertilisers
Finite resources — will run out if consumed faster than they form: fossil fuels, metal ores, minerals
Renewable resources — can be replenished: wood (if managed), crops, solar energy, wind energy
Recycling — processing used materials into new ones; reduces demand on finite resources and cuts energy use

sections.title: Sustainable Development
sections.text: Sustainable development balances the needs of today's population with the long-term health of the planet for future generations.
points: Definition — development that meets current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Reduce — use fewer resources in the first place; e.g. lighter product packaging
Reuse — use items again for the same purpose; e.g. refillable bottles
Recycle — reprocess materials into new products; e.g. melting aluminium cans for new cans
Renewable energy — switching to solar, wind, and hydroelectric reduces depletion of fossil fuels
LCA — Life Cycle Assessment evaluates environmental impact at every stage of a product's life

callout.label: Definition
callout.text: Sustainable development meets the needs of the current generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

sections.title: Mining and Environmental Impact
sections.text: Extracting natural resources has significant environmental consequences that must be weighed against societal benefits.
points: Habitat destruction — open-cast mining removes vegetation and destroys ecosystems
Pollution — mining waste and chemical runoff can contaminate soil and water
Land degradation — spoil heaps and quarries alter landscapes for decades
Phytomining — using plants to absorb metal ions; less destructive than conventional mining
Bioleaching — bacteria extract metals from low-grade ores; avoids large-scale excavation

keyTerms.def: A resource that will eventually run out — cannot be replenished
A resource that can be replenished naturally
Development that meets current needs without compromising future generations
Reprocessing a used material into a new product, saving energy and raw materials
A material obtained directly from the Earth — metal ores, fossil fuels, timber
A material made by chemical processing of natural resources, such as plastics or medicines
An evaluation of the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction to disposal

examTips: Metals are finite — they must be mined; recycling conserves them and uses far less energy.
Know the sustainable development definition — it often comes up in 6-mark questions and must be stated precisely.
Be able to distinguish reduce, reuse, and recycle — examiners look for correct use of all three terms.
commonMistakes: Saying wood is a finite resource — it is renewable if managed sustainably through replanting.
Confusing reusing (same purpose, same item) with recycling (reprocessed into a new material).
Treating all natural resources as renewable — metals, fossil fuels, and minerals are finite.
clozePassages: The Earth provides us with many natural resources including fossil fuels, metals, and fresh water. Some of these are finite (non-renewable) — they will eventually run out if we continue to use them at current rates. Others are renewable. Sustainable development means using resources to meet current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Reducing, reusing, and recycling materials are key strategies for more sustainable use of resources.

Recycling conserves finite resources and reduces energy use. Recycling aluminium uses only 5% of the energy needed to produce it from bauxite ore. Recycling copper, steel, and glass all save energy and raw materials compared to extracting and processing virgin materials. However, collection, sorting, and processing recyclables also requires energy and resources. Life cycle assessments help evaluate whether recycling is more sustainable than other options.

Humans obtain resources in various ways. Mining extracts metal ores and other minerals from the ground. Agriculture produces food and plant-based materials. Drilling extracts fossil fuels. These processes can cause environmental damage including habitat destruction, pollution, and land degradation. Phytomining (using plants to absorb metal ions from soil) and bioleaching (using bacteria to extract metals) are more sustainable alternatives for low-grade ores.

Life Cycle Assessment.intro: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction to disposal.
Life Cycle Assessment.mnemonic: "Every Manufacturing Use Disposes" — Extraction, Manufacturing, Use, Disposal — the four stages of an LCA in order.
Life Cycle Assessment.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Life Cycle Assessment
Image coming soon

sections.title: Stages of an LCA
sections.text: An LCA follows a product from cradle to grave, examining environmental inputs and outputs at each of four key stages.
points: Stage 1 — Raw material extraction — mining, drilling, quarrying; considers energy use and habitat damage
Stage 2 — Manufacturing and packaging — energy input, chemical use, water consumption, waste generated
Stage 3 — Use and transport — energy used during operation; emissions from delivery and distribution
Stage 4 — Disposal — landfill, recycling, incineration; considers emissions and resource recovery
Cradle to grave — LCA covers the entire lifespan, not just manufacture

sections.title: What LCA Considers
sections.text: LCAs measure a range of environmental impacts to give a comprehensive picture of a product's footprint.
points: Energy use — total energy consumed at each stage, usually expressed in megajoules
Water consumption — water used in manufacturing, cleaning, and agriculture
Carbon footprint — total CO₂ and equivalent greenhouse gas emissions across all stages
Waste and pollution — solid waste to landfill, liquid effluent, air emissions
Resource depletion — the rate at which finite materials are consumed
Comparative use — LCAs can compare two products (e.g. paper bag vs plastic bag) to identify the more sustainable option

sections.title: Limitations of LCA
sections.text: LCAs are powerful tools but have important limitations that must be considered when interpreting results.
points: Subjectivity — different companies may weigh factors differently, producing different conclusions from the same data
Commercial bias — companies can select which stages to include to make their product look more sustainable
Incomplete data — some impacts (biodiversity loss, social costs) are difficult to quantify
Cost and time — a full LCA is expensive and time-consuming to conduct
Not the full picture — LCAs focus on environmental impact and may not consider economic or social factors

callout.label: Limitations
callout.text: LCAs can be subjective — different companies may weigh factors differently. Can be used selectively to support a commercial argument. Numerical data may be incomplete.

keyTerms.def: An evaluation of the environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life
Total CO₂ (and equivalent) emissions from a product or process
Term for the full lifespan of a product, from raw material extraction to final disposal
The final stage of an LCA: landfill, recycling, or incineration of the product at end of life
The first LCA stage: mining, drilling, or farming to obtain the materials needed
A limitation of LCAs — value judgements about which impacts matter most can vary between assessors

examTips: LCA covers the WHOLE life of a product — from raw materials to disposal; always include all four stages.
Be critical of LCAs — they can be biased and involve value judgements; state this clearly in evaluate questions.
In compare questions, identify which stage makes the bigger difference and explain why — e.g. use phase vs manufacture.
commonMistakes: Saying LCAs are completely objective — they involve subjective judgements about what to measure and how to weight factors.
Forgetting the disposal stage — many students only consider manufacturing when asked about LCA stages.
Assuming a lower manufacturing impact always means a better LCA — the use phase can dominate (e.g. a long-lasting product with high energy use).
clozePassages: A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product from extraction of raw materials to disposal — often called cradle to grave. It considers extraction and processing of raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, and disposal. LCAs help compare the environmental impact of different products and identify stages where improvements can be made. Some stages are easier to quantify than others.

The stages of an LCA include: extraction of raw materials, manufacture and processing, distribution, use, and end-of-life disposal or recycling. At each stage, inputs of materials and energy are considered alongside outputs of waste and emissions. A product with a low manufacturing impact may have a high use-phase impact (e.g. energy consumption). LCAs help businesses make more informed decisions about product design and encourage sustainable choices.

LCAs have limitations. Some stages are difficult to quantify — for example, the environmental cost of land use or biodiversity loss. LCAs can be manipulated to favour a particular product by selecting which stages and factors to include. They are also time-consuming and expensive to carry out fully. Despite these limitations, LCAs are valuable tools for comparing the overall environmental impact of different materials and helping make more sustainable choices.

Water.intro: Water is essential for life and industry. Understanding how water is made safe to drink and the difference between potable and pure water is required for C10.
Water.mnemonic: "Silly Fish Can't Drink" — Sedimentation, Filtration, Chlorination, Desalination — the water treatment steps in order.
Water.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Water Treatment
Image coming soon

sections.title: Potable Water
sections.text: Potable water is safe to drink but is not chemically pure — it contains dissolved salts and minerals that do not harm health.
points: Potable ≠ pure — potable water is safe to drink but contains dissolved substances
Not 100% H₂O — contains dissolved salts, minerals, and sometimes fluoride; this is normal and safe
UK sources — surface water (rivers, lakes, reservoirs) and ground water (aquifers, wells)
Rainwater — naturally slightly acidic due to dissolved CO₂, but can be treated to make potable
Pure water — only obtained by distillation; too expensive for drinking water supply

sections.title: Making Water Potable
sections.text: Freshwater from rivers and reservoirs undergoes a three-stage treatment process before it is safe to drink.
points: Sedimentation — water is held in a large tank; heavy particles settle to the bottom by gravity
Filtration — water passes through sand and gravel beds to remove smaller particles and some bacteria
Chlorination — chlorine gas is added to kill remaining microorganisms and make water safe
Why this order? — removing particles first makes chlorination more effective and less chlorine is needed
pH adjustment — lime may be added to adjust pH; very acidic water corrodes pipes

sections.title: Desalination
sections.text: Desalination removes salt from seawater or brackish water to produce freshwater, but requires much more energy than standard treatment.
points: Distillation — seawater is boiled; pure water vapour is condensed; very energy intensive
Reverse osmosis — high pressure forces water through a semi-permeable membrane; removes salt ions
Energy cost — desalination uses far more energy than treating freshwater; expensive to operate
Global use — widely used in water-scarce regions such as the Middle East and parts of Africa
Not used in UK — the UK has sufficient rainfall and freshwater; desalination is uneconomical here

keyTerms.def: Water that is safe to drink — not necessarily pure
The removal of dissolved salts from seawater to make it drinkable
Adding chlorine to water to kill microorganisms
Allowing solid particles to settle out of water under gravity
Passing water through sand and gravel to remove fine particles
Using high pressure to force water through a semi-permeable membrane, removing dissolved salts
Underground rock layer that holds groundwater — a source of freshwater

examTips: Potable ≠ pure. Potable water contains dissolved substances but is safe to drink — make this distinction in every answer.
Chlorination kills microorganisms — it does NOT remove dissolved salts; those require distillation or reverse osmosis.
Always give the correct order: sedimentation → filtration → chlorination. Reversing these loses marks.
commonMistakes: Saying potable water is pure water — potable means safe to drink, not chemically pure (100% H₂O).
Confusing filtration (removes particles) with chlorination (kills microbes) — they are different stages with different purposes.
Saying distillation is used in UK water treatment — it is not; it is only used in desalination or laboratory settings.
clozePassages: Fresh water is a vital but increasingly scarce resource. It can be obtained from rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Before use, water must be treated to make it safe to drink. Sedimentation allows solids to settle. Filtration removes fine particles. Chlorination kills microorganisms. The treated water is potable — safe to drink. In some regions, desalination (removing salt from seawater) is used, but this requires large amounts of energy.

Water quality is assessed by measuring the concentration of dissolved substances and microorganisms. Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions from rocks. It is not harmful to health but causes scale in pipes and reduces the effectiveness of soap. Hard water can be softened by adding sodium carbonate to precipitate calcium ions, or by passing it through an ion exchange column. Distillation produces very pure water but is expensive.

Waste water from homes and industry must be treated before being returned to rivers. Sewage treatment involves screening, sedimentation, and biological treatment by bacteria that decompose organic matter. Sludge can be dried and used as fertiliser or digested anaerobically to produce biogas. Industrial effluent is treated to remove toxic chemicals before discharge. Good water management is essential for environmental protection and public health.

Alternative Metal Extraction.intro: Traditional metal extraction uses carbon reduction or electrolysis, but newer methods are being developed for low-grade ores and environmental reasons.
Alternative Metal Extraction.mnemonic: "Plants Burn, Bacteria Leach" — Phytomining (Plants Burn to give ash), Bioleaching (Bacteria produce Leachate) — two alternative extraction methods.
Alternative Metal Extraction.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Alternative Metal Extraction
Image coming soon

sections.title: Traditional Extraction
sections.text: Conventional methods work well for rich ores but become uneconomical and environmentally damaging for low-grade deposits.
points: Carbon reduction — metals below carbon in reactivity series (e.g. iron, copper) reduced by carbon in a furnace
Electrolysis — metals above carbon (e.g. aluminium) extracted using electrolysis; much more energy intensive
High-grade ores — traditional mining is economical only when ore contains sufficient metal percentage
Environmental impact — large-scale mining causes habitat destruction, pollution, and extensive land use
Depletion — high-grade ores are being used up; new methods needed for lower-grade deposits

sections.title: Phytomining
sections.text: Phytomining uses hyperaccumulator plants to draw metal ions from soil, offering a low-impact extraction route.
points: Hyperaccumulator plants — certain plants absorb unusually high concentrations of metal ions through their roots
Harvesting — the metal-rich plants are harvested when mature
Burning — the biomass is burned; the ash contains concentrated metal compounds
Metal extraction — metal is then extracted from the ash using conventional chemical processes
Advantages — useful for low-grade ores; less destructive than open-cast mining; can remediate contaminated land

sections.title: Bioleaching
sections.text: Bioleaching uses bacteria to chemically dissolve metals from low-grade ores, producing a metal-rich solution for further processing.
points: Acidophilic bacteria — specialised bacteria that thrive in acidic conditions break down metal sulfide ores
Leachate production — bacteria produce an acidic solution (leachate) containing dissolved metal ions
Metal recovery — metal extracted from leachate by electrolysis or displacement with a more reactive metal (e.g. scrap iron for copper)
Speed — bioleaching is slower than traditional smelting; may take months to years
Advantages — lower energy use, less landscape damage, suitable for ores too poor for smelting

keyTerms.def: Using plants to absorb metal compounds from soil, then burning to extract the metal
Using bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores
Rock containing only a small percentage of the desired metal
The acidic solution produced by bioleaching, containing dissolved metal ions
A plant species that absorbs unusually high concentrations of metal ions from the soil
Using carbon (coke) to reduce metal oxides to metals in a blast furnace — for metals below carbon in reactivity
A more reactive metal displacing a less reactive metal from its solution, used to recover metals from leachate

examTips: Phytomining = plants absorb metal → harvest → burn → extract metal from ash. Know this four-step sequence.
Bioleaching = bacteria produce acidic solution containing metal ions → extract by electrolysis or displacement.
Both are useful for low-grade ores where traditional extraction is uneconomical — state this as a key advantage.
Always mention the final extraction step — the metal still needs to be obtained from the leachate or ash.
commonMistakes: Confusing phytomining (plants) with bioleaching (bacteria) — they are completely different processes.
Forgetting the final step — metal still needs extracting from the solution or ash after bioleaching or phytomining.
Saying bioleaching produces the pure metal directly — it produces a leachate from which the metal must then be extracted.
clozePassages: Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal ions from low-grade ores in the soil. The plants are harvested and burned. The ash contains a higher concentration of the metal than the original soil. This method is less destructive than traditional mining and can be used on previously mined land. Bioleaching uses bacteria to extract metals from ores. The bacteria produce acidic solutions that leach out metal ions, which can then be processed to obtain the metal.

Bioleaching uses microorganisms to convert metal compounds in low-grade ores into soluble metal ions. The resulting solution, called a leachate, contains the metal ions. The metal can be extracted from the leachate by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis. Bioleaching is slower than traditional extraction but can be used on ores that would be uneconomical to process using conventional methods, reducing the need to mine high-grade ores.

Traditional metal extraction by smelting uses large amounts of energy and causes pollution. Phytomining and bioleaching are greener alternatives, particularly for low-grade ores. They cause less landscape destruction and use less energy. However, they are slower processes. As high-grade ores become depleted, these alternative extraction methods will become increasingly important. Recycling metals is also an important strategy to reduce the need for primary extraction.

Corrosion.intro: Corrosion is the degradation of metals by reaction with their environment. Rusting is the most common example.
Corrosion.mnemonic: "Iron Owns Water And Oxygen" — Iron corrodes when both Water And Oxygen are present — remove either one to prevent rust.
Corrosion.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Corrosion and Rusting
Image coming soon

sections.title: Rusting
sections.text: Rusting is the specific corrosion of iron, requiring both oxygen and water to occur, and produces hydrated iron(III) oxide.
points: Conditions required — iron needs BOTH oxygen AND water to rust; neither alone is sufficient
Product — rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O); orange-brown and flaky
Redox reaction — iron is oxidised (loses electrons); oxygen is reduced (gains electrons)
Saltwater accelerates rusting — salt acts as an electrolyte, speeding up the electrochemical corrosion process
Economic damage — rusting costs billions of pounds annually in structural and vehicle damage worldwide

sections.title: Prevention Methods
sections.text: Rust can be prevented by either creating a physical barrier that excludes oxygen and water, or by sacrificial protection.
points: Painting or oiling — creates a physical barrier preventing water and oxygen from reaching the iron surface
Galvanising — coating with zinc; zinc is more reactive than iron and acts as a sacrificial metal
Electroplating — coating with another metal (e.g. chromium) for corrosion resistance and aesthetic appeal
Sacrificial protection — attaching blocks of zinc or magnesium; they corrode preferentially, protecting the iron
Alloying — stainless steel contains chromium and nickel; chromium forms a protective oxide layer

sections.title: Sacrificial Protection in Detail
sections.text: Sacrificial protection works because a more reactive metal will corrode in preference to iron, even when the iron is exposed.
points: Reactivity principle — a more reactive metal corrodes preferentially over a less reactive one
Zinc on ships — zinc blocks are bolted to ship hulls; zinc corrodes instead of the steel hull
Galvanising scratch-proof — even if zinc coating is scratched and iron is exposed, zinc continues to corrode preferentially
Electrochemical process — the more reactive metal acts as the anode and is oxidised; iron acts as cathode
Replacement — sacrificial anodes must be periodically replaced as they are consumed

keyTerms.def: Degradation of a metal by reaction with its environment
Oxidation of iron in the presence of water and oxygen
Coating iron with zinc to prevent rusting
Attaching a more reactive metal that corrodes instead of the protected metal
The chemical name for rust — Fe₂O₃·xH₂O — formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water
An alloy of iron, chromium, and nickel that resists corrosion due to a protective chromium oxide layer
Using electrolysis to coat a metal object with a thin layer of another metal for protection or aesthetics

examTips: Rusting needs BOTH oxygen AND water — remove either to prevent it; mention this explicitly in exam answers.
Galvanising works by BOTH barrier AND sacrificial protection — explain both mechanisms for full marks.
Stainless steel resists corrosion because chromium reacts with oxygen to form a self-repairing protective oxide layer.
commonMistakes: Saying only oxygen causes rust — water is also needed; both must be present.
Forgetting that galvanising works by sacrificial protection even if the zinc coating is scratched — this is a key exam point.
Confusing electroplating (applying a thin metal layer by electrolysis) with galvanising (specifically zinc coating of iron).
clozePassages: Corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment. Rusting is the corrosion of iron — it requires both oxygen and water. The iron is oxidised to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Rusting causes significant economic damage to structures and vehicles each year. It can be prevented by keeping iron dry, painting, oiling, or coating with another metal such as zinc (galvanising) or tin.

Galvanising protects iron by coating it with a layer of zinc. Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it is preferentially oxidised — it provides sacrificial protection. Even if the zinc coating is scratched and iron is exposed, the zinc continues to corrode in preference to the iron. Sacrificial protection can also be provided by attaching blocks of a reactive metal such as magnesium or zinc directly to the iron or steel structure.

Methods of preventing corrosion include physical barriers that keep oxygen and water away from the metal surface. Painting, applying grease or oil, electroplating with a less reactive metal (such as tin-plating steel for food cans), and plastic coating all create barriers. Alloying iron with chromium and nickel produces stainless steel, which is resistant to corrosion. The chromium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, protective oxide layer on the surface.

Materials.intro: Different materials have different properties making them suitable for different uses. Understanding how structure determines properties is key to materials science.
Materials.mnemonic: "Ceramics Can't Compose Polymers" — Ceramics (brittle, hard), Composites (combined properties), Carbon fibre, Polymers (flexible) — the four main material types.
Materials.diagram:
🖼️
Diagram: Materials and Their Properties
Image coming soon

sections.title: Ceramics
sections.text: Ceramics are made from clay or sand heated to high temperatures, producing hard, brittle, heat-resistant materials used in construction and technology.
points: Formation — made from clay or silicon compounds fired at high temperatures; covalent/ionic bonding gives rigid structure
Properties — hard, brittle (crack rather than bend), high melting point, good thermal and electrical insulators
Soda-lime glass — made from sand (SiO₂), limestone, sodium carbonate; used for windows and bottles
Borosilicate glass — more heat-resistant than soda-lime; used in laboratory glassware and ovenware
Glass-ceramics — can withstand rapid temperature changes (thermal shock); used in hob cooktops
Examples — pottery, brick, cement, porcelain, silicon carbide (cutting tools)

sections.title: Composites
sections.text: Composites combine two or more materials to create a product with properties superior to either component alone.
points: Matrix and reinforcement — a composite has a matrix (surrounding material) and a reinforcement (embedded material)
CFRP — carbon fibre reinforced polymer: carbon fibres add strength; polymer matrix adds lightness and flexibility
Fibreglass — glass fibres embedded in a polymer resin; lighter than steel, used in boat hulls and car bodies
Reinforced concrete — concrete (good compression) reinforced with steel rods (good tension); used in construction
Dental composites — resin reinforced with glass or ceramic particles; tooth-coloured and durable

sections.title: Polymers and Smart Materials
sections.text: Polymers are long-chain molecules with versatile properties, and smart materials respond to changes in their environment.
points: Thermoplastics — soften on heating and can be remoulded; recyclable; e.g. polyethylene, PET
Thermosetting polymers — form permanent cross-links on heating; cannot be remelted; e.g. Bakelite, epoxy resin
Shape memory alloys — return to original shape when heated; used in medical stents and spectacle frames
Thermochromic materials — change colour with temperature; used in baby spoons and mood rings
Hydrogels — absorb large amounts of water; used in contact lenses, wound dressings, and agriculture

keyTerms.def: Hard, brittle material made from clay fired at high temperature
Material made from two or more materials combined to have improved properties
Long-chain molecule; many synthetic polymers used as materials (plastics)
A polymer that can be softened and reshaped by heating — recyclable
A polymer with permanent cross-links that cannot be melted once formed
A material whose properties change in response to external conditions such as temperature or light
A metal alloy that returns to a predetermined shape when heated above a transition temperature

examTips: Composites combine properties of their components — always explain what each component contributes (e.g. carbon fibre adds strength, polymer adds flexibility).
Ceramics are brittle — they crack rather than deform; this is a key difference from metals and polymers.
Be able to choose a material for a given use and justify your choice using specific properties.
commonMistakes: Confusing composites (two different materials combined) with alloys (two or more metals mixed together).
Forgetting that glass is a ceramic — it is made from silicon dioxide and has the typical brittle, hard properties.
Saying all polymers can be recycled — thermosetting polymers cannot be remelted once formed, unlike thermoplastics.
clozePassages: Different materials have different properties that make them suitable for different uses. Metals are strong, malleable, and good conductors. Ceramics are hard, brittle, and heat-resistant. Polymers are lightweight and can be moulded into shapes. Composites are made from two or more materials combined to give properties better than either alone. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer combines the strength of carbon fibre with the light weight and flexibility of the polymer matrix.

Glass is a ceramic material made by melting sand (silicon dioxide) with limestone and sodium carbonate. It is transparent, hard, and chemically resistant. Soda-lime glass is used for windows. Borosilicate glass has a low coefficient of thermal expansion and is used for laboratory glassware and cookware. Composite materials such as reinforced concrete combine the compressive strength of concrete with the tensile strength of steel rods to make a versatile building material.

Smart materials have properties that change in response to external stimuli. Shape memory alloys return to their original shape when heated, used in medical devices and spectacle frames. Thermochromic materials change colour with temperature, used in mood rings and baby spoons. Hydrogels absorb large quantities of water and are used in soft contact lenses and wound dressings. New materials are constantly being developed through research and nanotechnology.
